lead: Every quantum experiment ends with a number you can read off, and every quantum gate must be undoable. Two matrix tests capture those demands. A matrix equal to its own conjugate transpose is Hermitian. It has real eigenvalues, so it can stand for something measurable. A matrix whose conjugate transpose is its inverse is unitary. It keeps lengths and angles, so it can stand for a gate or a time step. Pauli X, Y, Z and Hadamard pass both tests, which is why they fill the first page of every qubit circuit.
prereq: You need matrices, eigenvalues and Dirac notation from 1.4 and 1.3.

blocks.text: The conjugate transpose of a matrix flips it across the main diagonal and complex-conjugates every entry. Write it A† and read it "A dagger".

blocks.where: A* is the matrix with each entry replaced by its complex conjugate; ᵀ means transpose, so entry (i, j) of A† is the conjugate of entry (j, i) of A.

blocks.text: A square matrix is Hermitian when A = A†. Real symmetric matrices are the easy case: conjugation changes nothing, so plain symmetry is enough. The 2×2 matrix A = [[1, i], [−i, 2]] is Hermitian. Conjugate the entries to get [[1, −i], [i, 2]], then transpose and you are back at [[1, i], [−i, 2]].

items: Every diagonal entry of a Hermitian matrix is real, because a = conj(a) forces its imaginary part to zero.
Off-diagonal entries come in conjugate pairs: entry (j, i) is the conjugate of entry (i, j).
For every vector |ψ⟩ the number ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩ is real when A is Hermitian.

blocks.text: That last point is why physicists care. A measurement gives a real number, so the operator for a measurable quantity, called an observable, must produce real values on every state. Energy, position and spin are all Hermitian operators. See Unit 2, Quantum measurement, for how those values become probabilities.

sections.h3: Real eigenvalues and the spectral decomposition

blocks.text: The eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix are always real. Here is the reason in two lines. Start from A|λ⟩ = λ|λ⟩. Multiply on the left by ⟨λ| to get ⟨λ|A|λ⟩ = λ⟨λ|λ⟩. The left side is real, the inner product ⟨λ|λ⟩ is real and positive, so λ must be real too.
Eigenvectors belonging to different eigenvalues are orthogonal, and after scaling they form an orthonormal basis of the whole space. That basis gives the spectral decomposition.

blocks.where: λᵢ are the real eigenvalues, |λᵢ⟩ are the matching orthonormal eigenvectors, and |λᵢ⟩⟨λᵢ| is the projector onto the direction of |λᵢ⟩.

blocks.text: Take the Pauli Z matrix, Z = [[1, 0], [0, −1]]. Its eigenvalues are +1 and −1. The eigenvectors are |0⟩ = (1, 0) and |1⟩ = (0, 1). The decomposition reads Z = (+1)|0⟩⟨0| + (−1)|1⟩⟨1|, which multiplies out to the same matrix.

The spectral theorem runs both ways: a matrix is Hermitian exactly when it has real eigenvalues and a full set of orthonormal eigenvectors. In matrix form A = UΛU†, where Λ is diagonal and real and U is unitary.
A square matrix U is unitary when U†U = UU† = I, where I is the identity. The conjugate transpose is the inverse.

blocks.where: U† is the conjugate transpose, I is the identity matrix, and U⁻¹ is the inverse of U.

items: Inner products survive: ⟨Ux|Uy⟩ = ⟨x|y⟩ for any vectors x and y.
Lengths survive, since a norm is the square root of an inner product with itself.
Every eigenvalue has modulus 1, so it sits on the unit circle as e^(iθ) with θ in radians.
A product of unitary matrices is unitary, and so is U†.

blocks.text: Keeping the inner product is exactly what a quantum gate must do. States have norm 1, and probabilities come from squared inner products, so a gate that changed lengths would break the sum of probabilities. Reversibility comes free: U† undoes U. That is why circuits are built from unitary gates only; see Unit 3, Single-qubit gates: Pauli, Hadamard and phase.

On a large space, a two-level unitary acts on just two basis states and leaves every other state alone. Any unitary on n qubits can be written as a product of two-level unitaries, which is how a compiler turns an abstract gate into hardware pulses. A one-qubit gate is the smallest case: a 2×2 unitary matrix.

sections.h3: Pauli and Hadamard: both properties at once

blocks.text: X, Y and Z are Hermitian, so they can be measured as spin along the x, y and z axes. They are also unitary, so they can act as gates. A matrix that is both satisfies U² = I, so applying it twice returns the original state. X, Y, Z and H each have that property; check Y² = I by hand once.

Do not assume the two labels come as a pair. The phase gate S = [[1, 0], [0, i]] is unitary, because its eigenvalues 1 and i both have modulus 1, but it is not Hermitian: S† = [[1, 0], [0, −i]] is not S. A real symmetric matrix such as [[2, 0], [0, 3]] is Hermitian but not unitary, since eigenvalues 2 and 3 do not have modulus 1.

figure.caption: From H = 1/√2 [[1,1],[1,−1]], the conjugate transpose returns H, so H is Hermitian; squaring gives I, with entries 0.5+0.5 = 1 and 0.5−0.5 = 0, so H is unitary. The eigenvalues are +1 and −1.

spec.aria: Worked example: the Hadamard matrix H = 1/√2 [[1,1],[1,−1]] gives H† = H so it is Hermitian, H² = I so it is unitary, and its eigenvalues are +1 and −1.

examples.question: The Hadamard matrix is H = (1/√2)[[1, 1], [1, −1]]. (a) Compute H†. (b) Show that H is Hermitian. (c) Compute H² and use it to show that H is unitary. (d) State the eigenvalues of H.
steps: All entries are real, so the conjugate H* equals H.
Transposing gives (H*)ᵀ = [[0.7071067812, 0.7071067812], [0.7071067812, −0.7071067812]], which is H again. So H† = H and H is Hermitian.
So H² = I. Because H† = H, this also says H†H = H² = I, so H is unitary and H⁻¹ = H† = H.
Eigenvalues: det(H − λI) = (0.7071067812 − λ)(−0.7071067812 − λ) − 0.5 = λ² − 0.5 − 0.5 = λ² − 1. Setting this to 0 gives λ = +1 and λ = −1.
Both eigenvalues are real and both have modulus 1, which is what the theory promises for a Hermitian unitary matrix.
examples.answer: H† = H, so H is Hermitian; H² = I, so H is unitary with H⁻¹ = H; its eigenvalues are +1 and −1.
examples.check:
import math
s = 1 / math.sqrt(2)
H = [[s, s], [s, -s]]
Hd = [[H[j][i] for j in range(2)] for i in range(2)]
print(round(s, 10))
print(Hd[0][0], Hd[0][1], Hd[1][0], Hd[1][1])
H2 = [[sum(H[i][k] * H[k][j] for k in range(2)) for j in range(2)] for i in range(2)]
print(round(H2[0][0]), round(H2[0][1]), round(H2[1][0]), round(H2[1][1]))

traps: Hermitian and unitary are separate tests. The real symmetric matrix [[2, 0], [0, 3]] is Hermitian but not unitary, and the phase gate S = [[1, 0], [0, i]] is unitary but not Hermitian. Check both properties, never one.
Forgetting the complex conjugate. With real entries the dagger is just the transpose, so students transpose and stop. Pauli Y gives the counterexample: Yᵀ = [[0, i], [−i, 0]] = −Y, but Y† = Y.
Order and reversal: (AB)† = B†A†, not A†B†. For a unitary both U†U and UU† equal I, but for a general matrix they differ.
Eigenvalues of a unitary matrix are not all 1. They have modulus 1, so they look like e^(iθ); the phase gate S has eigenvalues 1 and i.
The identity matrix is both Hermitian and unitary, so it never separates the two ideas. Pick a non-trivial matrix when you are asked for an example that is one but not the other.

quiz.q: Define A† and state the conditions for A to be Hermitian and for U to be unitary.
quiz.a: A† = (A*)ᵀ: conjugate every entry, then transpose. Hermitian means A = A†. Unitary means U†U = UU† = I.

quiz.q: Write the spectral decomposition of a Hermitian matrix and name its parts.
quiz.a: A = Σᵢ λᵢ|λᵢ⟩⟨λᵢ|, with λᵢ real eigenvalues and |λᵢ⟩ an orthonormal eigenbasis.

quiz.q: Why must every quantum gate be unitary?
quiz.a: A gate must keep the norm at 1 so probabilities still sum to 1, and must preserve inner products so angles between states do not change. A unitary matrix does both, and it is invertible with inverse U†, which matches reversible evolution.
Conjugate: [[2, 1−i], [1+i, 3]]. Transpose: [[2, 1+i], [1−i, 3]], which equals A. The diagonal entries 2 and 3 are real. So A is Hermitian.

quiz.q: Show that S = [[1, 0], [0, i]] is unitary, give S⁻¹ and its eigenvalues, and say whether S is Hermitian.
quiz.a: S† = [[1, 0], [0, −i]]. Then S†S = [[1, 0], [0, (−i)(i)]] = [[1, 0], [0, 1]] = I, so S is unitary with S⁻¹ = S†. Eigenvalues are 1 and i, both of modulus 1. S† ≠ S, so S is not Hermitian.

quiz.q: A matrix is both Hermitian and unitary. Prove that each of its eigenvalues is +1 or −1.
quiz.a: Hermitian gives A = A†; unitary gives A†A = I. Substituting, A² = I. If A|λ⟩ = λ|λ⟩ then A²|λ⟩ = λ²|λ⟩ = |λ⟩, so λ² = 1 and λ = ±1. Each value is real and has modulus 1, so both requirements agree.

quiz.q: Explain what a two-level unitary is and why it matters for building arbitrary gates.
quiz.a: A two-level unitary acts as the identity on all basis states except two, where it applies a 2×2 unitary block. Any unitary on a larger space can be written as a product of such matrices, so a gate is compiled into a sequence of small operations that touch two states at a time. A one-qubit gate is the smallest example.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gate compilers reduce an arbitrary unitary to a small hardware set using two-level decompositions plus a fixed library of one-qubit and CNOT gates. The Solovay–Kitaev theorem says this can be done efficiently to any target accuracy, which is why fault-tolerant designs count gate counts. Search for "Qiskit transpile basis gates", "Solovay–Kitaev theorem" and "Cartan decomposition two-qubit gates" to go further.
